#1985. Manchester United sack Michael Carrick 10 days before Liverpool showdown

Manchester United have sacked Michael Carrick as head coach 10 days before their next fixture, which is against Liverpool at Anfield.

As was widely expected, the 45-year-old has paid the price for the Red Devils’ atrocious start to the season, with the Old Trafford outfit winning just one of their first 10 Premier League games and sitting in the relegation zone during the November international break.

Fabrizio Romano reported the news via X on Thursday morning, with other media outlets then confirming it before an official announcement from the club was communicated.

As per Sky Sports, Mauricio Pochettino is expected to be named as Carrick’s successor, with Man United having an agreement in place with the Argentine – currently in charge of the USA men’s national team – to take over after their CONCACAF Nations League in the coming week.

Should that impending appointment be completed in the anticipated timeframe, the former Tottenham and Chelsea boss would be in place in time for the Red Devils’ visit to Anfield on Sunday 22 November.

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Although the practice of ‘new manager bounce’ isn’t exactly a scientific formula, a myriad of case studies – a few of which involve Man United – may have injected trepidation into Liverpool fans ahead of the grudge match in L4 on Sunday week.

Carrick himself took over a Red Devils team in turmoil last January and, in his first two games, oversaw wins over Manchester City and Arsenal, who ultimately finished second and first in the Premier League.

Eight years ago, after Jose Mourinho got the sack at Old Trafford following a comprehensive defeat at Anfield, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer triggered an immediate upturn in form which saw them pick up 25 points from a possible 27 in the top flight.

Managerial changes aside, Man United have an annoying habit of pulling out a result against Liverpool when it’s least expected. In January 2025, they were 14th in the table when they faced the table-topping Reds on Merseyside and came away with a 2-2 draw.

Iraola has already tasted defeat twice at Anfield this season (against Man City and Arsenal). Another on Sunday week would rankle the most of all, especially when our arch-rivals have been so abysmal over the past three months but conveniently trigger a change just in time for their visit to L4.

#1984. Why England fans booed Arsenal defender Ben White again after Croatia win

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Ben White returned to the England senior squad on Thursday night but received a hostile reception at Wembley.

The Arsenal defender came on as a substitute in the 78th minute of England’s 2-1 Nations League win against Croatia but was met with boos from a section of the crowd.

Thomas Tuchel has since defended White, stating that he should be in the squad. However, this raises questions as to why some England supporters have turned on the defender after he has continued to perform well for Arsenal.

The answer lies with the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.

He did not play in the first two group games for England and missed the last group game against Wales due to illness.

There were reports that White had fallen out with assistant manager Steve Holland, but neither the FA nor England management confirmed this was the reason he left.

Gareth Southgate later stated there were no problems between White and Holland and that White had simply withdrawn himself from selection after the tournament.

This meant that White would never play for England again while Southgate was still manager. Some fans were clearly upset by this, as they felt White was shunning his country.

When White returned under Tuchel in March 2026, he was met with a negative reaction. He was booed by the crowd when he scored his first-ever international goal against Uruguay. White was also booed in the same fashion against Japan.

He has since explained that supporters might view the situation differently if they knew the full story. However, he has chosen not to reveal the private details behind his departure.

Tuchel has shown little concern about White being affected by the controversy.

The England boss said after the win on Thursday that he had not heard any boos and praised White’s qualities, work ethic and desire to play for his country.

He believes White can help England win games and added that he has the backing of the coaching staff.

Arsenal fans will be unsurprised to learn that White is still a valuable asset for Mikel Arteta, offering defensive consistency and being able to play as a right or centre-back.

The bad press that White is receiving from England fans will not go away any time soon. However, he has not done anything to hurt his reputation at club level. The reasons why he left for the World Cup are personal.

The main focus for Arsenal will be getting him match fit again. As for the England fans, we shall see.

#1983. Arsenal Women vs London City Lionesses preview: Gunners face tough test at the Emirates

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Arsenal look to build on their recent win over Liverpool as they return to the Emirates Stadium but will face an impressive London City Lionesses side who are a potent attacking threat on their travels.

Renée Slegers’ team have struggled to convert their strong performances into points in the league this season. They have lost their last four WSL games at home, however, becoming the first team in WSL history to draw four successive games at home.

Their bad run must come to an end. They have taken just three points from their first nine league games so far this season, scoring a miserable total of 10 goals. However, they look like they have more in the tank and will need to be much more clinical in front of the goal.

The day also marks Slegers’ 50th game in charge of the WSL. The Dutch manager has only lost six league games so far this season, with only Chelsea having a better record from teams that have been ever-present in the division.

Arsenal can’t take their opposition lightly after London City’s impressive recent form. They have won two and drawn once in their last three away league games, scoring 12 goals.

Eder Maestre’s side has become a potent attacking force. Daniëlle van de Donk has provided four assists this season, and Delphine Cascarino has scored three goals and provided two assists.

Kadidiatou Diani can be dangerous. She has scored or assisted in all four of her league games away from home this season.

London City’s attacking prowess means they are a far different proposition to some teams Arsenal have faced at home. They have been in a positive situation for 62.7 per cent of their league minutes this season, the highest in the WSL.

Arsenal will have to deal with the attacking threats but look to utilise their ball possession better. Giving London City an opportunity to counter could make an already tough afternoon even tougher.

Alessia Russo comes into the game having found the net in her last three WSL games and will be key in converting Arsenal’s chances into goals.

The Gunners also showed their fighting spirit in their midweek clash against Barcelona. They drew 1-1 at Camp Nou to become the first side to take points off the Spanish giants in the Women’s Champions League at home since April 2024.

Slegers’ team will feel emboldened by that result but will have to change their tactics against London City.

They have won all seven games against Arsenal so far, scoring an impressive 22 goals and only conceding once. However, given London City’s recent away form, they will be hotly favoured.

They certainly have the quality to take all three points, but they must finally convert their dominance into a comfortable home win.

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Arsenal transfer interest in Alphadjo Cisse is starting to take shape. Arsenal are monitoring the development of AC Milan starlet Alphadjo Cissé, although his sensational start to the season could prove to be costly for Mikel Arteta.

The 20-year-old has made a blistering start to his Serie A career and attracted interest from a number of Premier League clubs after his impressive displays so far. Arsenal are reported to be interested.

The Gunners are among several clubs, including Brighton, keeping tabs on the player, according to Italian football news website Tuttomercatoweb. The striker is rumoured to be worth up to 60 million euros. That’s an eye-watering sum for a player who is just starting out in his professional career.

Cissé was signed by Milan from Hellas Verona in February 2026 but was allowed to finish the season on loan at Catanzaro.

Prior to joining the San Siro, he had already showcased his potential with six goals in 22 games in Serie B. He has made a huge impact since moving up to the top division.

Cissé has found the net five times in nine Serie A games this season. He has also chipped in with three goals in four Europa League games, making a total of eight goals in 13 games.

This has made him an important addition to the Milan squad. He is also versatile, as he can play as an attacking midfielder or higher up the park.

Arsenal may find his versatility attractive. Arteta likes players who can play in different positions and with injuries, and with a busy fixture list, he will want to have players who can do that.

The main issue could be that Milan are keen to keep their young star.

It is reported that the Italian club have turned down a verbal offer from Brighton and are looking to extend Cissé’s contract, which currently runs until June 2030.

This indicates that Milan is considering his future, rather than looking to make a profit. It also demonstrates just how quickly his reputation has developed.

Arsenal have the funds to target exciting young talent, but would they want to spend so much on Cissé?

There is no indication that he would be an instant replacement for Arsenal’s current attacking options. However, Cissé’s age, goal-scoring ability and versatility make him an interesting prospect.

This could be one to keep an eye on beyond January. Milan have little motivation to sell, and Arsenal might want to see how he develops before committing themselves.

Cissé has already hit the ground running in Italy and now needs to prove that his initial success can turn into something more consistent.

#1980. Max Dowman breaks Jude Bellingham record as Arsenal teenager makes England history

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Max Dowman has added another incredible achievement to his burgeoning career after becoming the youngest player to play for the England Under-21s.

The Arsenal youngster was introduced from the bench in Friday’s 1-0 friendly loss to Portugal at Ashton Gate. The 16-year-10-month-13-day-old player is over three months younger than Jude Bellingham was when he played his first game for the Under-21s.

Dowman replaced former Arsenal academy player Amario Cozier-Duberry in the 61st minute. He came on alongside debutant Trey Nyoni as England tried to shift the momentum of a challenging game.

An early strike from Afonso Moreira gave Portugal the lead in the 28th minute. An ineffective England team failed to respond. However, the replacements gave Lee Carsley’s team some late momentum.

Despite the hosts’ attempts to level the score, they failed to break down the Portuguese defence. The result means England have lost for the second game running. However, Dowman had much to be pleased with personally.

Dowman has added to his growing collection of records.

He became the youngest player to play in the Champions League, the youngest goalscorer in the history of the Premier League and the youngest to win the Premier League title.

Breaking Bellingham’s England Under-21 record is another significant step. It shows how quickly Dowman has progressed through the international age groups.

He has already made a big impression at Arsenal with Mikel Arteta’s love of giving younger players a chance, but Dowman will have some stiff competition for first team minutes.

Another positive is his progression on an international scale. He will improve both physically and tactically playing against older players and gain experience at a higher level.

England will host France in their next friendly on Monday, 16th November. Dowman will be hoping to feature after his instant impact on the record books.

Despite the disappointing result against Portugal, it was a landmark evening for the Arsenal players.

Dowman is already building a legacy at club level, but now he can add to his list of records by becoming an England Under-21 record holder.

At just 16, he has plenty of time to improve and show consistent performances to get more opportunities with the senior Arsenal squad.

Martin Ødegaard has spoken out about the speculation surrounding his future. He has stated he would like to stay at Arsenal for the future.

The captain has also admitted that talks about a new deal have not yet begun. Ødegaard is currently under contract until the summer of 2028. This leaves Arsenal with an important decision to make over the coming months.

Bayern Munich are being linked with an interest in the midfielder according to reports from Germany. The Bundesliga giants are said to be keeping their eyes on the player’s situation.

Speaking while on international duty with Norway, Ødegaard was quick to dismiss the speculation. He made it clear he is settled in north London and sees his future being at the Emirates Stadium.

There is no suggestion that the 27-year-old is seeking a move. Although comments do highlight a contract issue that Arsenal will be keen to resolve in the short term.

The Norwegian’s laid-back attitude should be encouraging for supporters.

He has made it clear that he is happy at the club and wants to stay here for the time being. This means that there is no need to panic.

However, Arsenal will have to get him to sign on the dotted line. Leaving his captain in the last year of his contract with no progress would cause an unnecessary distraction.

Since his permanent move from Real Madrid in 2021, Ødegaard has become a key player in Mikel Arteta’s plans. He has grown into a team leader and is one of the most influential players in the dressing room.

His importance has been shown by his inclusion in all 10 of Arsenal’s Premier League games so far this season. He has scored three goals.

This is a big improvement on last season, where he was hampered by injuries and failed to make much of an impact in front of goal.

There is little reason for Arsenal to consider losing their captain. He brings so much more to the team than just his technical ability and has been relied upon by Arteta to lead by example.

The midfielder was also pivotal in the 1-0 win over Hull City on 7 November, scoring the winner in the 72nd minute to give the league leaders three crucial points.

Arsenal have put themselves in a good position in the title race. Keeping their key players happy will be important in the second half of the campaign.

The Gunners will be focused on their game against Newcastle United on 21st November.

Arsenal fans have no real reason to panic at the moment, with the captain wanting to stay at the club and his comments suggesting he is happy.

However, it would be a good idea for the club to try and ensure his long-term future at the club. Ødegaard is still an important part of Arteta’s strategy, and ensuring he stays at the club would be a smart move.

#1977. Ex-Hungary captain hits out at ‘sobbing’ Andoni Iraola after Dominik Szoboszlai injury comments

A former captain of the Hungary national team has criticised Andoni Iraola for his treatment of Dominik Szoboszlai amid an injury concern to the Liverpool midfielder.

The 26-year-old sprained his knee in the first half of the 3-1 victory at Crystal Palace last weekend but continued playing until the 69th minute until he was replaced by Trey Nyoni.

The Reds’ head coach made a thinly-veiled plea afterwards for our number 8 to not feature for his country during this international window, with the Hungarian FA subsequently stating that they’ll defer any decision on his involvement against Georgia and Northern Ireland for as long as possible.

In quotes published by the print edition of Blikk (via Sport Witness), ex-Hungary goalkeeper Janos Csank blasted Iraola for not substituting Szoboszlai at half-time in the win over Palace.

The 80-year-old raged: “I was really annoyed. Szoboszlai went down on the pitch in the first half, and at half-time I was certain he wouldn’t come back on for the second half. Then I saw him standing there on the pitch, with black tape on his leg, his knee.

“Then the manager starts sobbing that he is injured. He should have been substituted straight away; they were leading 1-0. Half-time comes and then he sends him back on injured with his knee bandaged?! I’m losing my mind! I just don’t get it.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

As head coach of Liverpool, the club to whom Szoboszlai is contracted, Iraola is well within his rights to utilise the player as he sees fit, and any decision to send him back out for the second half would surely have been taken in consultation with the medical staff.

We admit that, if that had happened on international duty, we’d be pleading for Marco Rossi to exercise caution and substitute the 26-year-old immediately. Every stakeholder will inevitably shout the loudest in favour of their best interests.

In a similar vein, Reds supporters will hope that the midfielder isn’t deemed fit enough to play for his country in the coming week and instead recover for the Manchester United game the following Sunday, whereas he’ll be striving to prove his fitness in time to face Georgia on Saturday.

Szoboszlai has almost always been available during his three-and-a-bit years as a Liverpool player, although he’s had an injury-hit few weeks of late, having only recently overcome a thigh problem which resurfaced during the win at Brentford last month.

Everyone of a Reds persuasion will face a nervous wait over the next week or so to see whether Iraola will have any fresh injury worries once our season resumes in 10 days’ time. Fingers crossed that everyone on international duty gets back to Merseyside unscathed.

#1976. Ten things I hate about football (Part Two)

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Having put the boot into pitch-soaking preliminaries, flamethrowers, silly kick-offs, unpunished obstruction and ball-playing keepers in my previous article, I felt some of my frustrations with the modern game starting to dissipate. Not for long, though, as I raged against five other deeply annoying aspects of football today.

The continual expansion of non-domestic tournaments is a right pain.

Not only do the overblown Champions League and other Uefa-run competitions last far too long, they cause severe collateral damage to such venerable institutions as the FA Cup (1872) and what was the Football League (1888) until television moved the goalposts in 1992.

Where Uefa goes, of course, its equally power-hungry brothers in Fifa are bound to follow, with the money-making exercises known as the Club World Championship and the World Cup. As one friend, a football agnostic, said when invited to watch yet another match from last summer’s tournament: “I’m living in a world of pain.” Sorry, Walter. Gianni Infantino’s questionable leadership of both organisations has feathered a lot of nests while running the risk of killing the goose that lays the golden eggs.

Who didn’t love FA Cup replays? One of my fondest memories is the second replay of the Newcastle v Bolton fifth-round cup tie in the 1975-76 season. After drawn games home and away, the third match was played on neutral territory. The brainboxes at Lancaster Gate in London, which was FA HQ until 2000, presumably looked at a map of northern England and decided Elland Road was a fitting venue.

In those days, the words “neutral” and “Leeds” were seen in the same sentence as often as childcare and King Herod. After United finally vanquished the Wanderers, the brick-wielding West Yorkshire hoolies ambushed us on the way back to the railway station. Happy to say we also won that encounter . . .

Replays have been scrapped by degrees; from the fifth round onwards in 2019-20, then completely from 2024-25. Teams playing in Uefa competitions are given a pass to the third round of the League Cup and the “smaller” clubs who are essential to the health of football have been thoroughly shafted.

The chance of a money-spinning tie in front of 60,000-plus spectators has been greatly reduced, allegedly to ease fixture congestion. No longer can fans relish the vendettas that were often triggered by replayed ties.

Such occasions have been usurped by knockout competitions that reach the exciting bit only after a whole host of tedious league-phase matches. If that’s progress, you can stick it where the sun doesn’t shine.

Once television paid the piper, it was bound to call the tune. The Premier League is one of many competitions beholden to the billions of pounds offered for worldwide broadcasting rights. If Sky or TNT doesn’t want a match to start at 3pm on Saturday, the time will be altered. Supporters travelling almost the length of England are treated with contempt. This trend has spread like a plague from the top tier to all the lower divisions.

You might have a 700-mile round trip to the Amex or the Vitality but be a good chap, set off at midday on a Friday or a Monday for an 8pm kick-off. Book a post-match hotel while you’re at it. Because the last train home left before the match started. The atmosphere you generate is an essential element of the viewers’ experience, of course. To show how much your enthusiastic support is appreciated, we’ll charge only £30 a ticket. Just remember to be grateful . .

While TV has done spectators no favours, neither has it considered the sensibilities of referees. They had it relatively easy in the days when only the FA Cup final and the League Cup final were broadcast live. Yes, I doubt the man in black enjoyed hearing his parentage mocked by 50,000 screaming fans but he could just laugh it off.

Trial by television has now taken centre stage. With countless replays of debatable incidents in super slo-mo, there is no hiding place. Rentagob former players, who in their prime would have cheated without compunction to gain an advantage, queue up to find fault. They might not know the laws of the game but that won’t stop them grinding their axe.

I like goal-line technology. I hate marginal offside calls, when the judgment is based on which particular freeze-frame the jokers at Stockley Park decide to use.

Many decisions made by the man (or woman) in the middle are debatable. That doesn’t necessarily mean they are wrong. Though if Jarred Gillett is involved, they usually are.

One particular bit of foul play makes my blood boil. It is sneaky, cowardly and reckless. It is also rarely punished, because most referees seem unable to see what’s occurring.

We all know the scenario: an aerial pass is contested by two or more players. It is perhaps nine feet above the pitch. One player leaps for the ball, eyes fixed on it. Let’s call him Big Dan Burn, for instance. The other doesn’t fancy his chances of winning possession fairly. Let’s call him Kai Havertz . . .

Herr Havertz looks briefly at the ball, then assesses when Burn will jump. The German nudges, pushes or backs into the Colossus from Blyth while he is in mid-air. Down he crashes, in an uncontrolled descent dictated by the laws of physics.

The referee almost always sees nothing wrong. No free kick, no card, let the game flow . . . In one such incident Burn fractured a few bones in his back. After the final whistle, the detestable Arsenal manager ranted and raved because Anthony Gordon’s winning goal had not been disallowed. If only the lickspittle interviewer had mimicked Del Boy talking to Rodney and said: “Shut up, you tart!”

They say money talks. That’s certainly true in football, though Dylan was more accurate when he sang “money doesn’t talk, it swears” on It’s Alright, Ma (I’m Only Bleeding).

For as long as I can recall, the overwhelming trend has been: to the richest, the glory. In the 1960s Manchester United were financially bolstered by Louis Edwards, whose company supplied meat products of interesting quality to thousands of schools.

In the 70s Liverpool reaped the dividends of long-term investment by the Moores family, whose fortunes came from football pools and retailing. The Moores also had a stake in Everton, a big force in the 80s.

In the 90s Jack Walker, a Blackburn businessman, paid for a team to win the newish Premier League. Ten years later Roman Abramovich, a fine and upstanding Russian oligarch, rescued Chelsea from financial oblivion. He was forced to relinquish control after his pal Putin ordered troops to invade Ukraine.

Arsenal got into bed with Alisher Usmanov, another man who had made billions after the collapse of the Soviet Union. He was the club’s biggest shareholder by 2009. As a Gunner told me on the train up to London this month for the Fulham v NUFC game: “Thank goodness he left before the doo-doo hit the fan.”

Meanwhile, Abu Dhabi money was about to transform Manchester City from also-rans into the pre-eminent force in English football.

Newcastle United’s current owners almost certainly wanted to do the same when they bought the club five years ago. They have not been allowed that freedom, so far, though they have twice overseen Champions League qualification for the first time in a generation and the first Wembley cup final win since 1955.

Football is no longer sport in the true sense. The playing field has never been less level, the vested interests never more entrenched. The Premier League, Uefa and Fifa are all complicit in this lucrative merry-go-round.

Apologies for donning my rose-tinted spectacles . . . but some things were better in the good old days.

#1975. Agony and ecstasy for Newcastle United stars as 30,000 away fans take over Strawberry Arena

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Incredible scenes at the Strawberry Arena.

Saturday night in Solna, just north of the centre of Stockholm.

Bosnian fans taking over the Strawberry Arena.

An estimated 30,000+ of them in a 51,409 sold out capacity crowd.

A Nations League match between Sweden and Bosnia & Herzegovina that didn’t disappoint.

Sweden blew the visitors away in the first half with Newcastle United’s Anthony Elanga playing his full part, always a threat as he repeatedly ran at the opposition defence. Not always successfully but Elanga a key role in forcing Bosnia back and that pressure leading to goals.

The first one arriving inside five minutes, a great cross from the right delivered by Anthony Elanga and Svensson’s flick header seeing the fingertips of the keeper unable to stop the ball nestling in the far bottom corner.

Arsenal’s Gyokeres then adding two more, the second of which was a penalty just before the break that made it 3-0 at the halfway point.

It looked like a humiliating night in prospect for the visitors but the 30,000 plus Bosnian fans stayed with their team and inside two minutes of the restart Gigovic brought it back to 3-1.

Elanga was one of two substitutions made by Sweden on the hour mark but within a minute Bosnia had another goal, Kolasinac scoring to make it 3-2.

Brilliant scenes inside the Strawberry Arena as the away fans celebrated.

The final half hour saw Bosnia roared on by their supporters but despite throwing everything it wasn’t to be, as the final score was 3-2 to Sweden.

However, for all of those inside the Strawberry Arena, a night they will never forget with the incredible scenes on the terraces.

Newcastle United’s Amar Dedic played the full match and on a night that wasn’t a stellar one for either defence, he didn’t have the best of games.

After the 3-2 defeat, Amar Dedić said his Newcastle United teammate couldn’t believe the crowd, with 30,000+ Bosnian fans making up the majority of the 51,000 attendance: “My brother Elanga told me that this is truly special, that he’s never seen anything like it. I told him, ‘These are our fans; for us, this is normal.'”

Sports Dunia gave the Newcastle United pair the following ratings out of 10 and write-ups:

Anthony Elanga – 7: ‘Elanga’s first half was electric. He grabbed an assist with a pinpoint cross for Svensson’s opener. We also saw him test Martin Zlomislic with a driven shot from range. His dribbling always felt threatening even if not every move came off. Ten possessions lost show the risk in his game, but that chaos unsettled Bosnia’s defence. From our perspective his impact justified a strong rating despite an early substitution.’

🚨 SVENSSON MAKES IT 1-0 SWEDEN, EXCELLENT CROSS FROM ELANGA + SMART HEADER https://t.co/ECT4QXpwDI

— Polymarket FC (@PolymarketFC) November 14, 2026

Amar Dedic – 5.5: ‘We expected more from Dedic on both sides of the ball. He did get forward, producing shots and attempting a cross, but his end product was inconsistent. Defensively he struggled against Sweden’s transitions, often arriving late or getting dragged inside. One or two efforts from range flew harmlessly off target. His 88% passing was neat yet mostly safe and backward. Overall we felt he never imposed himself fully on the game.’

#1974. Lewis Hall opens up on his route to becoming Newcastle United and England first choice

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Lewis Hall is in brilliant form for England and Newcastle United.

The lifelong Newcastle United fan has now become clearly the best left-back that England have.

A huge game away to Spain tonight and Lewis Hall expected to be in the starting line-up having been the best player on the pitch when England beat Croatia 2-1 in midweek.

His career direction though could have been very different.

Lewis Hall began as a kid with Chelsea, where he came through the academy ranks playing in both midfield and defence as well, as he did with the England development teams.

He is such a talent with supreme confidence on the ball, you could imagine him having the ability to play anywhere on the pitch.

Left-back it was to be though and it was Thomas Tuchel who actually gave Lewis Hall his first taste of first team football when they were both at Chelsea.

Lewis Hall telling the official England media: “A lot of my game has been developed at left-back but I think I could play in midfield if I needed to…but as a career, I feel I have more ability at left-back just with the way we play at Newcastle United as it really suits my game with full-backs being involved. I feel I get loads of the ball in good areas and last season I worked on the defensive side of my game which is really important to me now. I like to get forward as well so when I’m getting the ball regularly, building from the back and getting the ball into the final third, I like to do that as well and create chances.”

Lewis Hall also talking about Ashley Cole, who he has worked with at both Chelsea and England: “He helped me a lot when I played towards the end of my spell at Chelsea. He gave me a lot of advice and he tries to help me out now. Especially with how good of a player he was, and in my position, he’s someone who I know that any advice he gives me is something I can take and look to use. There’s a lot of things he did with me with regards details to positioning, but everyone’s different. He said to me that he could give me tips on how he would defend certain situations but there might be other situations where I would defend differently because of the profile of player that I am compared to him. But something he’s always told me is to be myself and trust my ability, and any advice I get along the way to just take it and use it.”

Lewis Hall also talking about his first experience of working under Thomas Tuchel at Chelsea, the now England boss handed him a first team debut in an FA Cup match in January 2022 when Hall became Chelsea’s youngest ever player in the competition: “I was 17 at Chelsea when I first trained with the first team and I just remember him and his staff being really welcoming to me…I think they realised what a big thing it was for a young player, because there was a couple of us who came up at the time. I remember his sessions were really good, a lot was possession-based which I really enjoyed and he was a good person to me and gave me my debut. Without that, it probably wouldn’t have given me the confidence to kick-on from there, so I’m grateful for that but right now I want to focus on here. I’m a completely different player now, so I’m not sure if that means anything now.”

#1973. Cristiano Ronaldo tribute party hilariously ruined with help of Newcastle United star

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

The Cristiano Ronaldo tribute party hilariously ended in disaster.

The Estádio Municipal de Braga hosting what was intended to be a celebration of the selfish prima donna’s international career.

It had always been about Cristiano Ronaldo rather than the team.

The 41-year-old embarrassingly walked out of the Portugal camp in September after he was told he would not start the in the Nations League away match against Denmark.

Cristiano Ronaldo was given a token £215 fine and 30-day suspension by Portugal.

Fast forward less than two months later and ahead of the reverse fixture with Denmark, he was at it again.

Rather than doing things properly, Cristiano Ronaldo retired from international football via a video he posted on his social media last week. No advance warning given and Portugal coach Jorge Jesus later revealed that Ronaldo would have been picked for these Uefa Nations League games against Denmark and Wales in November.

With his out of the blue announcement, Portugal then quickly made this Saturday night Portugal v Denmark match all about Cristiano Ronaldo.

All of the Portugal players and the mascots walked out wearing a ‘Ronaldo 7’ shirt.

The fans displayed the word ‘Ronaldo’ in the top tier of one of the stands.

A banner that translated as ‘thank you, captain’, plus a similar message appearing on the scoreboard in the seventh minute.

How brilliant it was then that this all ended in disaster.

Pierre-Emile Hojbjerg scored a penalty just before half-time, then Rasmus Hojlund scored twice in eight minutes to make it 3-0 with more than half an hour remaining.

With 73 minutes on the clock Newcastle United striker William Osula came off the bench and within a minute had won a free-kick towards the right wing. The resultant free-kick seeing Joachim Andersen head the fourth and the Cristano Ronaldo fan club left in tears as his tribute well and truly had fallen apart.

Osula came close to adding a fifth but unlucky to see his late effort blocked.

Bernardo Silva did get a no consolation goal for Portugal in the third minute of added time but the final 4-1 humiliating scoreline at home, was such a fitting tribute to Cristiano Ronaldo.

#1972. Bonera believes Milan Futuro were not ready for first season: “Some thought it was easier”

Daniele Bonera has revisited his time as the head coach of Milan Futuro, revealing his belief that the team wasn’t ready to compete.

The Futuro project was launched ahead of the 2024-25 season to give Milan a ‘second team’ to allow their young talents to develop at a level above that of the Primavera league. They started in Serie C but were relegated in their first season.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

The decision was taken to sack Bonera as the head coach given the on-field issues, even though they were competing against experienced sides with a very young side. Massimo Oddo followed him, before the club chose to go with Sergio Navarro this summer, who has the Futuro in third.

Bonera was interviewed by Fanpage and he reflected on that period with the B-team and what he learned from it even despite the rough results, with his comments relayed by MilanNews.

“Milan Futuro was a great opportunity for growth. Perhaps we weren’t clear – and I’m part of this – about the level of Serie C. I had an idea of ​​it, but some thought it was easier,” he said.

“The squad had been built with expectations that were too high compared to what the league is. I don’t think that structure, at that time, was ready to tackle that type of league. On an individual level, however, I felt very comfortable. Starting at home was a positive thing.

“The biggest challenge was understanding which players you actually had available. Some were promoted to the first team, others were dropped, and still others were sent to the Primavera. We had guys who perhaps weren’t playing with us and then came back up.

“From an individual growth perspective, we worked very well in some situations. After a couple of years, we saw the individual value of guys like Camarda, Bartesaghi, Liberali, and Jimenez grow. The value of the players wasn’t in question.

“I think the problem was primarily structural: it’s not always the coach who’s the problem, but the way you do things and the direction you want to take.”

#1971. A message for Newcastle United fans ‘Please positively support the team’

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

A message for my fellow Newcastle United fans.

There is a sound in sport more discordant than the pure roar of opposition.

Our recent Everton home match showcased it.

It was loud, and it was often, and it was heard by football fans all around the world. It is the sound of a home crowd turning on its own. At St. James’ Park, that sound has been heard with increasing frequency in recent matches—sharp, collective, and unmistakable.

Newcastle United fans, among the most passionate and historically loyal in English football, have at times directed their frustration not solely at the referee or the visiting side, but at the men in black and white who wear the shirt they revere. And while discontent is a fan’s prerogative, the practice of booing one’s own players carries consequences that extend far beyond a single afternoon’s dissatisfaction. It damages the athletes who must perform under it’s weight and it slowly erodes the very reputation of the supporters who claim to love the club most.

Consider first the players. Professional footballers are not automata. They are human beings operating at the outer edge of physical and psychological demand, often carrying the accumulated pressure of ownership expectations, media scrutiny, and the weight of a city’s hopes. When the crowd that once lifted them now turns its voice against them, the effect is not motivational theatre. It is corrosive.

Confidence is a fragile commodity in sport; once fractured in public, it is slow to mend. A player (especially a young or new player) who hears the boos after a misplaced pass or a missed chance does not suddenly discover a higher gear. More often he tightens, second-guesses, and retreats into the safety of safer choices. The game becomes smaller. Risk—the very quality that produces moments of brilliance—becomes something to be avoided.

History offers quiet lessons. The great teams of the past were not immune to periods of struggle, yet the bond between player and supporter was understood as reciprocal. Kevin Keegan’s side of the mid-1990s rode waves of belief that were almost tangible. Even in disappointment, the underlying current remained one of shared purpose.

When that current reverses, the club’s identity begins to fray. Players notice. They speak of it privately, if not always publicly. They adjust their body language, their willingness to demand the ball, their instinct to press high. What the stands intend as accountability can register on the pitch as abandonment. For those of us that have played footy at any level (or any public activity) – loud criticism seldom inspires, it creates a heavier load.

There is also the matter of reputation—the intangible but real currency of a club’s supporters. Newcastle United fans have long been celebrated for their loyalty through lean decades, for the sheer volume and colour they bring to the occasion, for the sense that the club and the city are inseparable. That reputation is not automatic. It is earned, season after season, through constancy of support that does not evaporate when results turn. Booing one’s own players, particularly in sustained fashion, risks rewriting that narrative. Outside observers—pundits, rival supporters, potential recruits—begin to form a different picture: of a crowd that is quick to turn, of an atmosphere that can become hostile even to those fighting in the same colours. Perception hardens. The next talented midfielder weighing a move, the young academy graduate deciding whether to commit his future, the manager assessing the environment he would inherit—all of them factor atmosphere into the equation. A club that once marketed itself on the passion of its people can find that passion reinterpreted as volatility.

None of this is an argument for silence or passive acceptance of mediocrity. Criticism is legitimate. I would argue, and I believe that most would agree, a team of players can inspire the crowd but that the reverse is true also. A crowd can create positive energy that propels the team on the pitch. It is a symbiotic relationship – and its this relationship that can make the home field a fortress. A negative reaction from the crowd can also beget poorer play on the pitch. Yes, boards, managers, and players should be held to account. But there is a distinction between demanding better and actively undermining those currently charged with delivering it. The former can be expressed through measured reaction, through pointed but constructive noise after the final whistle, through the continued presence and volume that still says “this matters.” The latter—booing in real time—sends a different message: that the relationship is conditional, and that the players are no longer considered part of the collective struggle. And when coming from the Gallowgate, arguably the most passionate fans anywhere, their negativity sets the tone for all.

Sport at its best creates a temporary community in which strangers become, for ninety minutes, something closer to allies. That community is tested when results fail. How it responds in those moments reveals its character. Newcastle United fans have, through far darker periods than the present, demonstrated a capacity for loyalty that borders on the heroic. The question now is whether that tradition will be preserved when the going is merely difficult rather than desperate. The players will answer on the pitch. The reputation of the fans will be answered in the stands—by the choice of what sound they choose to make when the team needs them most.

I know the players make a lot of money. I also know that buying the ticket gives each fan the right to express themselves in their own way. But, actions have consequences, and, in my opinion, booing your own players is like “keeping up the whippings until morale improves.” 🎙️ THE MAG PODCAST Ep 15: Fulham frustration, Newcastle United’s season report card and Relegation fears Listen to the latest episode of The Mag Pod! #1970. Here is how to watch for free online as Stadium of Light hosts huge Sunderland v Newcastle United Women derby

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

It is Sunderland v Newcastle United Women this Sunday afternoon at the Stadium of Light.

Newcastle United Women and Tanya Oxtoby getting ready for this derby.

The Stadium of Light hosting at 2pm on Sunday 15 November.

You can watch this Sunderland v Newcastle United Women derby for free online here at the official WSL2 site.

After seven rounds of league matches Newcastle United Women are unbeaten and top of the second tier on 19 points from a possible 21, three clear of Sunderland.

It may seem a little premature when this derby clash is only the eighth match of the league season BUT a win for Newcastle United Women and they will surely already have one hand on the Title AND most importantly, promotion to the Super League.

It is only a 22 match season in the second tier and a win for Newcastle United Women would see them go six points clear of Sunderland with only 14 rounds of matches remaining, plus a minimum of at least five points clear of any other team, potentially more depending on how other results go on Sunday.

Only top spot guarantees automatic promotion to the Super League, as the teams that finish second and third in Women’s Super League 2 will play off for the right to face the team that finishes second bottom of WSL1 and a chance at promotion.

Tanya Oxtoby is manager of Newcastle United Women and has been talking ahead of facing Sunderland.

Ahead of this massive derby, Tanya Oxtoby on Newcastle United Women facing Sunderland: “Two teams in really good form with really good squads. It’s a great challenge for us and that’s what we’ve been talking about; the fact that we want to be pushed and we want to see how good we can be. We should embrace moments like this because it’s a positive thing.”

Tanya Oxtoby on what she wants from her players: “We talk a lot about making sure we’re proactive, and that we’re not being reactive to a certain game or a certain instant. We want to make sure that we’ve got our tools in the toolbox to be able to deal with that, and we’ve been working on that from pre-season, all the way through to now. We are who we are, and we want to go out and play our style of football, but it will be against a really good side. We’re going to have to think outside of the box in terms of solving problems when they appear.”

Tanya Oxtoby on the Newcastle United fans: “They’re the best and you saw that on the weekend. We have the best fans and I know that they will come out in their numbers. I know that they will bring their voices. For us, our responsibility in that is to make sure that we put on a good performance they can be proud of, like we did last weekend.”

Best of luck to the lasses when they take on the Mackems this afternoon.

#1969. The Newcastle United players who are part of the problem and…those who are part of the solution

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Here below I have listed the Newcastle United players who are part of the problem.

A separate list of those who are part of the solution…

Whilst also the Newcastle United players who could fall either way.

Simply what I have seen with my own eyes and so using my expert judgement…

Newcastle United players who are part of the solution

Lukas Hornicek, Lewis Hall, Amar Dedic, Malick Thiaw, Dan Burn, Lewis Miley, Sean Steur, Fabian Schar (as a back up for rest of season)

Newcastle United players where it is unfair/impossible to judge as not seen enough of them

William Osula (he has still only started 12 Premier League matches for NUFC), Aladji Bamba (0 PL starts), Nico Gonzalez (8 EPL starts for NUFC), Ewen Jaouen (0 PL starts), Bazoumana Toure (0 EPL starts), Matias Fernandez-Pardo (4 EPL starts)

Newcastle United players who are part of the problem (and can they be part of the solution (marked Yes, No, Maybe?)

Tino Livramento – Yes. We know he is a quality player BUT can he ever stay fit?

Sven Botman – Maybe. Was absolutely brilliant in his first (2022-23) season when United had best defence in the Premier League. Two big operations/injuries and hasn’t been able to get back to that level on a consistent basis. So far.

Joelinton – No. May seem a bit harsh but he is another who has been heavily impacted by injuries, plus he is now into his 30s. I think as well that if Newcastle are to play a mobile passing game, our “Only cost forty million” Brazilian doesn’t fit in.

Jacob Ramsey – Maybe.  Has shown at times he has the quality but not able to put a run of form together of any length as a starter, injuries not helping. I think by the end of this season we will know either way. With United losing the likes of Tonali and Bruno, Ramsey should be making a starting eleven position his own.

Joe Willock – No. He was brilliant in the 2022-23 then had really bad time with injuries. We have seen at times the necessary quality and impact this season in glimpses but he isn’t able to do enough to be a certain starter.

Harvey Barnes – Maybe. Always the issue with Harvey, if he can get into goalscoring positions he is Newcastle’s best finisher. When he doesn’t though, his overall contribution is rarely enough to deserve a starting place. Last season Barnes started 19 Premier League matches and came off the bench in 18 of the other 19. It feels very much like he represents the team/squad going backwards as he starts week in week out now. I do like him but can he show enough to be more than a supersub?

Anthony Elanga – Maybe. Started the season on fire AND looking a real goal threat. Unlucky to then pick up an injury in training. I think it is possible he can prove his doubters wrong but a case of hope for the best but fear the worst.

Jacob Murphy – No. A bit like Willock and into his 30s now. His standout season of 2024-25 in now history. Has produced a few quality moments this season but doesn’t produce enough over whole matches to be a starter.

Yoane Wissa – Maybe. Very much like Elanga, a case of hope for the best but fear the worst.

When I talk about those who I have listed as part of the solution, it isn’t necessarily that I see them as world beaters, more a case of I think they are definitely good enough to at least perform at a certain level which we now need.

Obviously there weren’t many of them that I could list and Schar is only as back up for this season, whilst with Dan Burn he turns 35 in May and so realistically, he could hopefully do another full season in 2027-28.

What we clearly need is for some of those who in the ‘impossible to judge yet’ to come through and prove themselves as time goes on.

Whilst more immediately, we really need some of those in the ‘part of the problem’ list above, to prove themselves real assets very soon AND prove the doubters wrong!

#1968. “It’s a special place” – Liverpool confirm Anfield return for James Milner

Liverpool FC have confirmed on Thursday that James Milner will return to Anfield in 2027.

Signed on a free transfer from Manchester City in 2015, the former Reds midfielder spent eight years on Merseyside and became vice-captain under Jurgen Klopp, winning the Premier League and Champions League among other trophies in his time with the club.

The 40-year-old closed out his playing career at Brighton, announcing his retirement this summer after setting the record for the most Premier League seasons appeared in (24 consecutively from 2002/03 to 2025/26).

As announced via liverpoolfc.com on Thursday lunchtime, Milner is the first player to be confirmed for the next Liverpool Legends match, which takes place against Inter Milan at Anfield on Saturday 27 March 2027, with proceeds going towards the LFC Foundation.

The Reds’ former vice-captain said of his participation in the fixture: “I’m thrilled to have the chance to pull on the red shirt again and step back out at Anfield. It’s a special place, and playing there in front of the supporters is a feeling like no other.

“What makes the legends match so special is that it’s about more than football. It’s a chance to give something back to the fans while supporting the work of the LFC Foundation. I’m delighted to be the first to sign up and can’t wait to be part of it.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

The news of Milner’s participation in the 2027 Legends match is sure to go down a treat with Liverpool fans who adored him for his humility and commitment to the cause in his eight years as a Red, along with his excellence as a player.

The Yorkshire native was renowned for setting exceptionally high standards within the playing group and enjoyed near-annual domination of the infamous pre-season lactate test, and he commands universal respect among his peers and the wider football community.

The Reds were lucky enough to be the club that he represented more times than any other, with 322 of his 903 senior appearances coming for the Merseysiders (Transfermarkt).

He’ll now get to line out in a Liverpool shirt at Anfield once more, and while it mightn’t be in a competitive fixture, the reception won’t be any less rapturous for a player whose supreme attitude characterised a glorious era for LFC.

As ever, it promises to be a wonderful occasion in which thousands of pounds will be raised for a most worthy cause, and Kopites will get to enjoy seeing many former greats of the club return for one afternoon.

#1965. Rising Newcastle United stars experience harsh Swedish lessons with the Young Lions

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

The Young Lions had a thrilling 3-2 victory against the Netherlands on Wednesday.

However, a different story when the England Under 18s ran into Sweden this weekend in their second of three matches in Valencia.

Rising Newcastle United stars Roman Dowell and Kyran Thompson started against Sweden.

An attacking player, Kyran Thompson recently turned 17 and has been in brilliant form for the Newcastle United Under 18s and Under 21s so far this season. He decided to leave Arsenal and join Newcastle this summer gone.

Whilst 16-year-old Newcastle United goalkeeper Roman Dowell (pictured at the top of this report) is making great strides at NUFC. Like Kyran Thompson, Dowell has also been in great form for both the Newcastle United Under 18s and Under 21s this season.

At the Oliva Nova venue in Valencia the Young Lions given some harsh Swedish lessons.

There were no real signs of what was to come in a pretty even uneventful opening half.

However, the Young Lions swiftly found themselves 2-0 down in no time after the break.

Roman Dowell left badly exposed by those in front of him, with Leonel Eklund scoring shortly after the restart and then Marlon Ebietomere made it 2-0 only minutes later.

Then with 17 minutes to go it was more of the same, Sweden going 3-0 when Eklund grabbed his second goal.

Roman Dowell played the full match, whilst his NUFC teammate Kyran Thompson was taken off just before the hour mark.

Some tough lessons to be learnt and for the United pair and their England teammates, at this early stage of their careers sometimes you learn more from a defeat such as this one than you do when you are winning.

Final score: Sweden Under 18s 3 England Under 18s 0

England: 13 Roman Dowell (Newcastle United), 3 Calvin Diakite (Chelsea), 5 Marlow Barrett (Manchester City), 6 Tyrese Noubissie (RC Strasbourg), 7 Ryan Kavuma-McQueen (Portsmouth, loan from Chelsea), 8 Hugo De Lisle (Leicester City), 12 Riley Ebho (Chelsea), 14 Kyran Thompson (Newcastle United), 16 Reon Smith (West Ham United), 17 Oliver Boast (Tottenham Hotspur), 20 Erik Farkas (Liverpool).

Substitutes: 23 Jacob Watson (Manchester United) for Diakite 24’, 11 Jeremy Monga (Swansea City, loan from Manchester City) for Kavuma-McQueen 46’, 18 Max Little (Southampton) for De Lisle 46’, 21 Jerome Abbey (Wolverhampton Wanderers) for Noubissie 59’, 9 Jashayde Greenwood (Chelsea) for Thompson 59’, 10 Samuel Alker (Leeds United) for Farkas 59, 15 Gabriel Sambou (Chelsea) for Ebho 71’, 19 Teddie Lamb (Manchester City) for Boast 71’

Niclas Füllkrug has again looked back on his time at AC Milan, joking that he ‘didn’t forget how to play football’.

Füllkrug joined Milan midway through the 2025-26 season on loan from West Ham and it was hoped that he could boost their Scudetto hopes, if not at least get them over the line in the top four battle. However, he scored just once and ultimately was not bought permanently.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

The German headed back to Werder Bremen in the summer, and has been in remarkable form since. He has scored nine goals in the Bundesliga which makes him the top scorer, and 13 goals in 11 games across all competitions, at an average of one every 64 minutes.

As a result, he was called up by coach Jurgen Klopp for the final two UEFA Nations League group stage matches against Serbia and the Netherlands. Speaking at a press conference, he revisited his short stint with the Diavolo.

“I was never unhappy during my time abroad. I’m very grateful for those experiences because there’s so much more to life than football. Of course, football is very important, but when you live abroad, you can still separate your personal life from your professional one,” he said (via MilanNews).

“I took away many positive memories from those two years. The main problem was that I struggled to stay in shape. I didn’t forget how to play football during that time.”

#1963. Rumoured Liverpool transfer target has been told to find a new club; he left Van Dijk bemused

One player who’s recently been linked with a move to Liverpool has reportedly been told that he’s free to leave his current club.

Two years on from being first linked with Malo Gusto, the Reds are understood to have maintained their interest in the Chelsea full-back and even made enquiries about him during the summer (TEAMtalk).

The same outlet reported that the Blues are seemingly holding out for a world-record fee for a right-back, which is currently held by Achraf Hakimi when he joined Paris Saint-Germain for €68m (then £60m) in June 2021.

According to Si Phillips Talks Chelsea, Xabi Alonso has told the French defender that ‘it is time he finds a new club’, with the ex-Liverpool midfielder preferring to put his trust in Marco Palestra and Josh Acheampong for the long-term.

It’s claimed that there have been ‘no fallouts’ from Gusto apparently being told that he’s surplus to requirements at Stamford Bridge, with the message being delivered to him ‘respectfully’.

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

The 23-year-old made a name for himself at Anfield just a couple of weeks ago, but not for the most positive of reasons.

The Chelsea right-back melodramatically threw himself to the ground after mild contact from Virgil van Dijk, who simply looked bemused by the Frenchman’s reaction, and he also petulantly waved his boot at the assistant referee in a futile attempt to get Bradley Barcola yellow-carded.

Those actions certainly didn’t do anything for his popularity among the natives, and it seems indicative that Alonso is apparently prepared to jettison him only a quarter of the way through his first season as Blues manager.

With all due respect to Gusto, Liverpool’s efforts to bolster their right-back options in the medium-term would be better served by trying to secure a permanent transfer for Ronald Araujo, who’s been excelling in that position since joining on loan from Barcelona in August.

It’d definitely make a lot more sense than paying upwards of £60m for the Stamford Bridge defender, especially if Jeremie Frimpong and/or Conor Bradley were to regain form and fitness in the second half of this season.

#1959. Why West Ham’s Fulham Defeat Gives Scott Parker Plenty To Be Pleased About

West Ham United were beaten 1-0 by Fulham in a behind-closed-doors friendly on Thursday, but I don’t think the result matters at all. If anything, losing by just one goal to Premier League opposition when we’ve got ten players missing on international duty is no shame whatsoever.

According to ExWHUEmployee, reporting through The West Ham Way, the match was arranged to give Scott Parker an opportunity to assess some of his players and help others build up their match fitness. No team sheet has been made public, so we don’t know exactly who featured.

What I’m particularly impressed by is how quickly Parker has organised and sorted this out. He’s barely been in the job five minutes, yet he’s already managed to arrange a friendly against Premier League opposition, presumably using his Fulham connections to get it done. That’s exactly the sort of proactive approach needed to drag the club back up the league table.

The bit I found particularly interesting was the emphasis on getting players up to fitness.

From that point of view, I’d have thought Soungoutou Magassa and Edson Álvarez would be prime candidates to have participated in the game. Alphonse Areola would also be an obvious beneficiary if he’s recovered sufficiently from his recent injury.

It’s also important for Parker to have a look at some of the other academy goalkeepers, particularly given the concerns over Fin Herrick’s fitness and the recent poor form of Mads Hermansen.

I’d rather hope Lewis Orford played some part in the game as well. He’s not getting nearly enough first-team football, and this would have been an ideal opportunity to show the new manager what he can do.

And, as I wrote earlier this week, the international break is going to afford Pablo the opportunity to try to impress the new Hammers manager.

Parker omitted the Brazilian striker from his first two matchday squads altogether, so a friendly like this could have been particularly useful for him.

We already knew that Parker’s preparations would be disrupted by the international call-ups, but he’s clearly not prepared to sit around waiting for everybody to return.

He’s taken a situation where ten players are unavailable and turned it into an opportunity to assess the rest of his squad against decent opposition.

I wouldn’t be remotely concerned about the 1-0 defeat. We don’t know who played, how many substitutions were made or even whether Parker was particularly interested in winning the match. Hopefully those details will be revealed by Ex later today?

For all we know, he may have learnt more from this game than he would have from a comfortable victory against weaker opposition.

It’s a thumbs up from me for Parker being proactive, particularly so early in his West Ham managerial career.

The only question is whether he’ll arrange another friendly next week before the Championship resumes against Preston.

#1958. West Ham-Linked Rangers Giant Features In Spain Victory

West Ham United transfer target Ryan Naderi was handed a starting place for Czechia against Spain in Thursday night’s UEFA Nations League encounter, which ended in a 2-0 victory for the Spanish.

The 6ft 4in Rangers striker, who has recently been linked with a January move to West Ham, played 66 minutes before being substituted. Spain took the lead through an Álex Baena penalty in the 39th minute, with Marc Pubill adding a second deep into stoppage time.

There was another West Ham connection to the match, with Tomáš Souček returning to international action as an 85th-minute substitute as Marin covered earlier today. Former Hammers Vladimír Coufal and Alex Král were also in the Czech starting line-up.

As Claret & Hugh reported yesterday, West Ham have been linked with Naderi following his impressive start to life at Rangers.

The 23-year-old has reportedly attracted interest from several clubs, although Rangers are understood to be reluctant to sell their striker during the January transfer window. Spain’s victory leaves them with five wins from five Nations League fixtures.

That sets up a particularly interesting encounter with England at the Metropolitano Stadium in Madrid on Sunday evening. The three lions spluttered to a 2-1 victory against Slaven Bilic’s Croatia last with Harry Kane scoring the winner from the spot.

The two sides are competing for top spot in Group A3, with the match kicking off at 7.45pm GMT.

Meanwhile, from a West Ham perspective, it is encouraging to see Souček back on the pitch following his recent injury problems, even if his involvement was limited to the closing stages.

#1957. Reports: Spurs and Juventus call Milan as on-loan midfielder continues to shine

AC Milan made the decision to loan Youssouf Fofana out in the summer window, and he is attracting interest from clubs around Europe.

Fofana’s situation ended up being quite a dramatic one. He was excluded from the plans by Ruben Amorim and seemed set to join Lyon on loan, but that fell through on deadline day. A move to Turkey didn’t materialise, but Sevilla stepped forward and managed to get a year-long loan deal done.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Since moving to Spain, Fofana has found his best form again. Having played nine LaLiga games for the Andalusian side so far, he has four goal contributions to his name, with one goal and three assists.

Calciomercato.com cite TEAMtalk and Spanish sources, who claim Fofana is attracting the interest of clubs like Tottenham and Juventus. They have already initiated preliminary discussions with Milan to assess the feasibility of a deal for next summer.

The club coached by Roberto De Zerbi has reportedly made concrete moves, beginning initial dialogue with Milan management, while Juve were linked in the summer and are still looking for midfield reinforcements.

For their part, Milan remain interested in listening to any offers that may arrive, considering that Amorim is still firmly in charge and has already expressed his opinion that the Frenchman is not a fit for his style and system.

The Rossoneri value the midfielder at around €15m, according to reports from abroad, and are waiting for interested clubs to make more concrete moves ahead of next season.

Sevilla meanwhile would not be able to pay the cost of the player’s wages, but would like to negotiate with Milan to extend their relationship with Fofana beyond this one-year loan, attempting to set up a permanent deal next summer.

#1956. Shrewd appointments usher in new era of reconciliation | West Ham News

Very slowly, with each new hire, be it high profile such as a head coach, or a less visible appointment behind the scenes, West Ham United is travelling in a new direction. The combative era of Sullivan and Brady calling supporters their ‘customers’ and riding roughshod over fan opinions seems well and truly in the past.

Their new hire – head of supporter services and fan engagement (she’ll never get that job title on a business card) Arsenal’s Khali Parsons is a sign of the direction of travel as the Club attempts to heal ten years plus of division between owners and supporters that has been a corrosive backdrop to the football club’s history since before the move from Upton Park.

Nothing, of course, can change the hugely unpopular sale of the old ground and the dissatisfaction over the ‘rented home’ which the club now occupy, but there does appear to have been some serious ‘listening’ going on rather than the scant lip service paid to supporters’ grievances by Karren Brady in the bad old days.

According to westhamworld.co.uk“Parsons will officially take up the role in January 2027 and will also become the club co-chair of West Ham’s Fan Advisory Board, replacing Paul Stringer, [Chief Marketing and Media officer] who is filling the position on an interim basis….Her arrival comes at an important time for West Ham, with the club’s senior leadership structure changing significantly and supporter trust one of the issues the new hierarchy has openly acknowledged needs rebuilding.”

Cult Hero Martin in his playing days at West Ham – now goal keeping coach for u21’s

Indeed, the news also that former Hammer David Martin is to return to the club as u21 goal keeping coach could be seen as further news of a return to a club better in touch with, and more comfortable with it’s own heritage.

Not quite sure how it will feel as a West Ham fan, all of this unity after so many years of protest. Heaven help us if we also start winning games again: We really will have to pinch ourselves.

#1955. West Ham Ticket Row: A Bit Of Pettiness? I’m All For It

West Ham United’s ticketing arrangements for the forthcoming Championship clash with Bristol City have caused controversy, but I have to say I’m firmly on the Hammers’ side with this one. If there’s an element of tit for tat involved, I don’t have a problem with it at all.

Bristol City supporters might not particularly like the situation, but there is some history between the two clubs when it comes to ticket allocations. During the FA Cup meeting in January 2024, Bristol City took their full allocation of around 9,000 tickets at the London Stadium, resulting in thousands of West Ham season-ticket holders having to move from their usual seats.

That caused considerable frustration at the time, with the West Ham United Supporters’ Trust seeking clarification from the club over the arrangements. So if the current situation feels like a bit of payback, I can certainly understand why.

One thing West Ham’s relegation to the Championship has provided is a real reality check when it comes to the treatment of travelling supporters.

In the Premier League, there was at least some collective understanding that away supporters shouldn’t be completely fleeced. The Football Supporters’ Federation’s original Twenty’s Plenty campaign eventually helped bring about the £30 away-ticket cap, which has remained in place since 2016.

It wasn’t perfect, and £30 was still more than supporters had originally campaigned for, but at least there was a limit.

That protection doesn’t exist across the Championship, and we’re now seeing the difference.

Take West Ham’s trip to Birmingham City in December, for example. According to the club’s official ticket information, adult supporters will be charged £37.50 for the privilege of watching the Hammers at St Andrew’s.

And it definitely feels like Championship clubs are treating us like absolute mugs.

When West Ham roll into town, we’re seen as a cash cow. Clubs know we’re going to bring a substantial travelling support, and it increasingly feels as though they’re happy to make the most of it.

Of course, I understand that Championship clubs have their own financial pressures, but that doesn’t make it any easier for supporters who are already spending a fortune travelling around the country.

I don’t have a problem with West Ham looking after our own fans, even if that means upsetting a few visiting supporters along the way.

Perhaps there’s a little bit of pettiness involved, but realistically, I don’t mind that either.

We’re West Ham, and the club should be looking after our fans. That ought to be the priority, particularly when supporters have been asked to put up with so much since dropping into the Championship.

And any Bristol City fans who don’t like it probably should look at their own club’s conduct when we played them in the FA Cup.

I don’t particularly want to see football clubs getting into an endless argument over ticket allocations, and ultimately I’d prefer supporters everywhere to be treated fairly.

But when it comes to this particular situation, I’m not going to criticise the West Ham hierarchy for giving a bit back.

Sometimes tit for tat is exactly what it looks like, and on this occasion, I’m perfectly happy with it.

#1952. Scott Parker’s ‘training session reveal’ shows clean break with Nuno’s strategy | West Ham United

With key players absent on international duty, these mid-international break training sessions are challenging for coaching staff who are keen to improve the team but of course don’t get to drill the whole squad.

West Ham United, though, with their reduced circumstances this season, have fewer players away than in the ‘old days’ of the Premier League thanks to player departures and others – like skipper Jarrod Bowen – simply being overlooked by their national coaches.

Yesterdays ‘inside training’ video shows clear blue water between the old days of Nuno Espírito Santo and the new-era Scott Parker training session. The very public participation of former ‘discards’ Edson Alvarez and Soungoutou Magassa – both featured from the outset along with perennial discard Maxi Cornet – shows Parker’s pledge to wipe the slate clean has being carried out.

Integrated and back in full training along with Edson Alvarez: Soungoutou Magassa

From the video evidence yesterday I’d say it is clear those days are long gone. Magassa has already started one game – hooked at half time – but I’d wager either the Frenchman or his Mexican midfield colleague, once upto speed, will be putting in an appearance in a reshaped Parker side this autumn: as the FLW article concludes:

“Hammers fans have long been calling for Alvarez and Magassa to be given a chance to solve their side’s midfield problems, and with the club’s hierarchy seemingly sharing that view, Parker should focus on reintegrating the duo over the international break.”

#1951. Scott Parker Reunion Could Be Key to West Ham Defensive Deal

No sooner had Scott Parker been appointed as West Ham’s ‘promotion specialist’ manager than stories surfaced linking him with the recruitment of former players.

Reports linking West Ham with C J Egan-Riley are unlikely to disappear anytime soon, with the former Burnley defender continuing to attract attention following his rapid development this season.

Egan-Riley enjoyed a breakthrough campaign previously under Scott Parker, establishing himself as one of the Championship’s standout young defenders and helping Burnley secure promotion back to the Premier League.

A move to the London Stadium would carry several attractions. Not only does Parker know the player well from their time together at Burnley, but Egan-Riley would also qualify as a home-grown player, an increasingly valuable asset for West Ham who are looking to balance squad registration requirements.

Parker has consistently praised the defender in the past, and stated he was a key player for him in the Championship. He was instrumental in the defender’s development, giving him a prominent role in Burnley’s promotion-winning side. His composure on the ball, ability to play across the back line and potential for further improvement make him the type of profile West Ham are expected to target.

Defensive stalwart for Scott Parker’s West Ham?

The central defender chose Marseille ahead of West Ham in 2025, who secured his signature on a free transfer after the expiry of his Burnley contract, meaning any transfer fee received would represent a substantial profit on their investment.

Having been a bit part player at the French club in his first season, following a squad overhaul in the summer he is now a regular starter and the data shows he has maintained a 93% pass completion in Ligue 1. The 23 year old ranks as one of the leagues most accurate passers in his position.

There is also reason to believe Marseille would be willing sellers. The French giants have made no secret of the fact that they will need to generate funds through player departures during the January transfer window due to ongoing financial issues. West Ham have enjoyed a productive relationship with Marseille over the years, with deals for Dimitri Payet, Emerson and Nayef Aguerd demonstrating that negotiations between the two clubs are far from uncommon.

The structure of any potential deal, be it an initial loan or a straight transfer, is yet to emerge. Either way, if the Hammers can persuade the defender to play a part in their quest for promotion they would be adding a young, home-grown centre-back who appears far from reaching his full potential.

I have been a season ticket holder since the late eighties, so experienced the highs and lows of being a West Ham supporter. I previously wrote for OLAS and have contributed to a number of football publications in the past.
